title: Spiral Matrix
directAnswer: Return every element of an m×n matrix in clockwise spiral order. The clean simulation walks with a direction vector plus a visited set (O(mn) space). The canonical interview answer keeps four boundary pointers — top, bottom, left, right — and peels one edge at a time, shrinking the boundary inward, using O(1) extra space.

remember.formula:
top, bottom = 0, m-1 ; left, right = 0, n-1
while top<=bottom and left<=right:
    walk top row L→R, top++
    walk right col T→B, right--
    if top<=bottom: walk bottom row R→L, bottom--
    if left<=right: walk left col B→T, left++
rules: Use **four boundary pointers** (top/bottom/left/right) and peel one full edge per step, then move that boundary inward.
Guard the **bottom row and left column** with `if top <= bottom` / `if left <= right` — without them a single leftover row or column is traversed twice.
Loop condition is `top <= bottom AND left <= right` — the spiral ends the instant the boundaries cross.
It's m×n, **not** necessarily square — track rows (m) and columns (n) separately; mixing them up is the top bug.
Append exactly **m·n** elements total. If your output length isn't m·n, a boundary update or a guard is off by one.
whenToUse: Traverse a grid in a non-row-major order (spiral, diagonal, zigzag)
Output count is fixed (m·n) and you're peeling layers inward
You need O(1) extra space on a grid walk
antiSignals: Plain row-by-row or column-by-column scan → just nest two loops, no spiral machinery
You need shortest path / connectivity on the grid → that's BFS/DFS, not boundary peeling
Rotation or reflection by a fixed angle → transpose + reverse (Rotate Image)
Random access to the k-th spiral element → derive a formula, don't simulate the whole walk
remember.takeaway: A spiral is just four directed edge-walks repeated on a shrinking rectangle. Hold the rectangle in four pointers, peel one edge at a time, and contract the matching boundary — the same boundary-as-state idea powers Spiral Matrix II, diagonal traversals, and any 'peel the outer layer' grid problem.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manage several moving boundaries at once without double-counting cells, and whether you spot that the leftover middle row/column needs an explicit guard.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Omitting the `if top <= bottom` / `if left <= right` guards before the bottom-row and left-column walks, so a single remaining row or column gets emitted twice on odd-sized matrices.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State up front that the answer has exactly m·n elements and that the only subtlety is the guards on the final two edges — then explain why a non-square middle strip is where the double-count happens.

problemStatement:
Given an `m x n` `matrix`, return ***all elements of the matrix in spiral order***.

Spiral order means: start at the top-left, walk **right** across the top row, **down** the right column, **left** across the bottom row, **up** the left column, then repeat one ring deeper until every cell is visited.
constraints: The matrix may be rectangular (m ≠ n is allowed)
understanding: Read the grid like you'd peel an onion: trace the outer ring clockwise, then the next ring in, until nothing's left. The catch is stopping each edge-walk at the right cell so you never revisit one — especially on the innermost row or column.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the matrix square?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Not necessarily — it's m×n. I'll track row bounds (top/bottom) and column bounds (left/right) separately so rectangles work.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which direction does the spiral go?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Clockwise, starting top-left: right, down, left, up. Counter-clockwise would just reorder the four edge-walks.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the matrix be a single row or single column?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — a 1×n or m×1 input is the case the boundary guards exist for. Without them that lone strip gets traversed twice.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should I return for the smallest input?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A 1×1 matrix returns its single element. The total output is always exactly m·n values.

examples.explanation: Outer ring clockwise (1,2,3,6,9,8,7,4) then the lone center 5.
3×4 rectangle: top row, right column, bottom row reversed, left column up, then the inner row 6,7.
A single cell — the spiral is just that element.

approaches.name: Direction Vector + Visited Set
approaches.whenToMention: A solid first pass that's easy to reason about — mention it, then trade the visited grid for boundary pointers to hit O(1) space.
hints: Think of a turtle walking the grid. It goes straight until it would step off the edge or onto a cell it already visited — then it turns right.
Encode the four directions as (dr, dc) vectors in clockwise order: right (0,1), down (1,0), left (0,-1), up (-1,0). Cycle through them with `dir = (dir + 1) % 4` on each turn.
Keep a visited[m][n] grid. Take m·n steps; before each move, if the next cell is out of bounds or visited, rotate the direction. Record and move.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Exactly m·n cells are emitted, each with O(1) work and at most one turn → O(m·n) time. The visited grid is m·n booleans → O(m·n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Simulate a walker that always goes straight until blocked, then turns right. 'Blocked' means the next cell is either off the grid or already visited.

**Why a visited grid makes this easy to get right.** The hard part of a spiral is knowing when to turn. With a `visited[][]` marker the rule is dead simple: try to step forward; if that cell is out of bounds or already marked, rotate the direction clockwise and step instead. You never have to reason about *where* the boundary is — the visited cells form it for you, and the turn rule is uniform for all four sides.

**Why the direction vectors cycle cleanly.** Listing the moves in clockwise order — right, down, left, up — means a single `dir = (dir + 1) % 4` performs every turn. The walker takes exactly `m·n` steps; on each, it either continues or makes one right turn, so the loop is bounded and terminates precisely when the grid is full.

**Why we don't ship it.** It allocates an m×n visited grid — O(m·n) extra space for a problem that has an O(1) solution. It's a great way to *explain* the spiral, but the boundary-pointer version encodes the same turning logic in four integers instead of a whole grid.
approaches.insight: The visited set is doing one job: telling the walker where the wall is. Once you notice the walls are always four straight lines forming a shrinking rectangle, you can replace the whole grid with four numbers — that realisation is the bridge to the optimal solution.

dryRun.intro: Walker starts at (0,0) heading right; it turns clockwise whenever the next cell is off-grid or visited.

code.python:
def spiralOrder(self, matrix: list[list[int]]) -> list[int]:
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    seen = [[False] * n for _ in range(m)]
    dirs = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
    out = []
    r = c = d = 0
    for _ in range(m * n):
        out.append(matrix[r][c])
        seen[r][c] = True
        nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
        if not (0 <= nr < m and 0 <= nc < n) or seen[nr][nc]:
            d = (d + 1) % 4
            nr, nc = r + dirs[d][0], c + dirs[d][1]
        r, c = nr, nc
    return out

approaches.name: Four Boundary Pointers (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Describe it as 'peel the top row, right column, bottom row, left column, then shrink the rectangle' and call out the two guards.
hints: Hold the un-emitted region as a rectangle defined by four lines: top, bottom, left, right. Each spiral step consumes one full edge of that rectangle.

Walk the top row left→right (then top++), the right column top→bottom (then right--), the bottom row right→left (then bottom--), the left column bottom→top (then left++). Repeat while top≤bottom and left≤right.
Before the bottom-row and left-column walks, guard with `if top <= bottom` and `if left <= right` — on odd dimensions a single strip remains and would otherwise be emitted twice.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each cell is appended exactly once across the four edge-walks → O(m·n) time. Only four integer pointers and the output list (which is required, not auxiliary) → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Track the un-visited region as a rectangle with four boundaries and peel one edge per move, contracting the matching boundary inward after each.

**Why four pointers replace the whole visited grid.** The unvisited cells always form a rectangle, and a rectangle is fully described by four numbers: `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`. Each spiral step walks one complete edge of that rectangle, then moves its boundary one step inward (`top++` after the top row, `right--` after the right column, and so on). The boundaries themselves encode 'where have I been', so the O(m·n) visited grid collapses to O(1) state.

**Why the bottom row and left column need guards.** After peeling the top row and right column, you might be left with a single remaining row (when `top == bottom`) or a single remaining column (when `left == right`). The first two edge-walks already consumed those cells. Walking the bottom row again when `top > bottom`, or the left column when `left > right`, re-emits cells you've already output. The guards `if top <= bottom` and `if left <= right` are exactly the check that says 'there's still an unconsumed row/column here'. This is the one subtlety the problem is really testing.

**Why it's optimal.** You still touch each of the m·n cells once — you can't do better, every element must be emitted — but you carry only four integers of state. Same time, minimal space, and the structure generalises directly to Spiral Matrix II (fill instead of read) and ring-by-ring problems.
approaches.insight: The leap from the previous approach is recognising the visited region is *always a rectangle*, so four numbers fully describe it. Representing a moving frontier by its boundaries rather than by marking every visited cell is a recurring space-saving trick — the same instinct that turns an O(n) seen-set into two pointers in sliding-window problems.

pitfalls: Dropping the `if top <= bottom` / `if left <= right` guards — double-emits the middle row/column on odd dimensions.
Using m for columns or n for rows — breaks immediately on rectangular input.
Forgetting to update a boundary (e.g. no top++) — infinite loop, never terminates.

commonMistakes: Omitting the bottom-row / left-column guards, double-counting cells on odd-sized or single-strip matrices.
Swapping rows and columns — reading n from matrix.length instead of matrix[0].length.
Forgetting to shrink a boundary after walking its edge, causing an infinite loop.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the bottom/left guards
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When only one row or column remains, the top-row and right-column walks already consumed it. Walking the bottom row / left column again re-emits those cells — your output is longer than m·n.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Confusing rows and columns
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On a rectangular matrix, matrix.length is the row count (m) and matrix[0].length is the column count (n). Using the wrong one for the boundary indices walks off the grid or stops early.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not advancing a boundary
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each edge-walk must be followed by shrinking its boundary (top++, right--, bottom--, left++). Skip one and the while condition never tightens — the loop spins forever or re-reads the same edge.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(matrix[top][c]);
// forgot top++  → top row re-walked next iteration
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for (int c = left; c <= right; c++) out.add(matrix[top][c]);
top++;
